title: If You Cant Solve a Problem, Make It Bigger
author: Admired Leadership
summary: The article introduces systems thinking as a tool for problems that resist conventional, piece-by-piece solutions. Using a roommate dish-washing dispute as an extended illustration, it shows how analyzing the whole interconnected system — rather than the individual complaints and remedies — reveals that the true root cause (the act of dish-washing itself) was hidden from view, and that eliminating that root element (paper plates) solves what years of schedules and confrontations couldn't. The piece's broader claim is that leaders facing a genuinely stuck problem should widen their lens to the entire system of relationships and incentives rather than continuing to attack the visible symptoms.
points: The dish-washing roommate example operationalizes systems thinking: the fix worked only once the root element (washing itself) was identified and eliminated, not managed.
The article's diagnostic question is specific and reusable: what element, if changed, changes everything else in the interconnected system?
Root-cause elements in team/organizational problems are named explicitly — reporting relationships, metrics, rewards, processes, and timelines among them.
quotes: Systems thinking views problems and their components as a whole rather than just a collection of its parts.
Applying systems thinking to this problem suggests examining each feature, element, and factor and the relationships between them.
From this perspective, the answer lies in eliminating the need to wash the dishes. Using paper plates is a solution that remains hidden to anything other than systems thinking.
The premise in systems thinking to solve problems is this: Changes in any part of the interconnected system can lead to changes in other parts, often in unexpected ways.
So, the next time you confront a problem no one can seem to solve, consider making the problem bigger by incorporating systems thinking.
